title: Φαλακρὸς ἱππεύς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 343 (= Perry 375). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Φαλακρός τις τρίχας ξένας τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κορυφῇ περιθεὶς ἵππευεν.
sentences.tr: Phalakros tis trichas xenas tēi heautou koryphēi peritheis hippeuen.
sentences.l: A certain bald man, having set another's hair about his own crown, was riding.
sentences.i: A bald man put a wig of another's hair on his head and went riding.
sentences.n: τρίχες ξέναι, 'hair belonging to another', is the Greek for a wig. ξένας is planted here to be picked up in his own retort below, where the same word means 'strange'.

sentences.t: Ἄνεμος δέ φυσήσας ἀφείλετο ταύτας· γέλως πλατὺς δὲ τοὺς παρεστῶτας εἶχεν.
sentences.tr: Anemos de physēsas apheileto tautas· gelōs platys de tous parestōtas eichen.
sentences.l: And a wind, having blown, took these away; and a broad laugh held the bystanders.
sentences.i: But a wind blew and carried them off, and a great laugh took hold of the bystanders.
sentences.n: ἀφαιρέομαι in the middle is 'take away from, deprive of'. Greek regularly makes the feeling the agent — the laughter 'holds' the onlookers rather than they it. δέ stands third in its own clause (γέλως πλατὺς δέ), later than the usual second place.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος εἶπε τοῦ δρόμου παύσας· « Τὰς οὐκ ἐμὰς τρίχας τί ξένον φεύγειν με, αἳ καὶ τὸν ἔχοντα ταύτας, μεθ’ οὗ καὶ ἐγεννήθησαν, κατέλιπον ; »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos eipe tou dromou pausas· « Tas ouk emas trichas ti xenon pheugein me, hai kai ton echonta tautas, meth’ hou kai egennēthēsan, katelipon ; »
sentences.l: And he said, having stopped from his course: « The hair that is not mine — what is strange in its fleeing me, which left even the man who had it, with whom indeed it was born? »
sentences.i: And he reined in and said: « The hair was never mine — what is strange in its running from me, when it deserted the very man it belonged to, the man it was born with? »
sentences.n: τί ξένον governs an accusative and infinitive: 'what is odd about the hair fleeing me?' ξένον answers the ξένας of the first line — the hair was another's, so there is nothing strange in its going, and one Greek word carries both senses. παύσας is the ACTIVE participle with the genitive τοῦ δρόμου, with its object unexpressed: he brought his mount to a stand from its course, where the middle παυσάμενος would have said only that he himself left off.

sentences.t: Ὅτι μηδεὶς λυπείσθω ἐπὶ συμφορᾷ ἐπελθούσῃ· ὃ γὰρ γεννηθεὶς οὐκ ἔσχεν ἐκ φύσεως, τοῦτο οὐδὲ παραμένει· γυμνοὶ γὰρ ἤλθομεν, γυμνοὶ καὶ ἀπελευσόμεθα.
sentences.tr: Hoti mēdeis lypeisthō epi symphorāi epelthousēi· ho gar gennētheis ouk eschen ek physeōs, touto oude paramenei· gymnoi gar ēlthomen, gymnoi kai apeleusometha.
sentences.l: That no one is to grieve at a misfortune that has come upon him; for what a man, on being born, did not have from nature, that does not stay by him either; for naked we came, and naked we shall depart.
sentences.i: The story shows that no one should grieve at a misfortune that has come upon him; for what a man was not born with from nature does not stay by him either — naked we came, and naked we shall go.
sentences.n: The moral opens with a bare Ὅτι, 'that', and Ὅτι cannot begin a sentence any more than English 'that' can: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, so the literal line leaves the fragment as it stands and the idiomatic line supplies 'the story shows'. ἐπέρχομαι is the regular verb for a misfortune's arrival. The closing clause is a moralist's commonplace rather than anything the fable itself said.
